endorsements.quote: Additionally, the use of AI in medical decision\u2011making or patient access to care must be clearly communicated to patients, who should retain the right to make informed choices regarding AI\u2011assisted care.

Physicians should retain clinical authority over AI\u2011generated recommendations but should not bear full responsibility for AI\u2011driven errors when the system is appropriately deployed within its intended use case.

Liability frameworks must reflect AI\u2019s collaborative role in clinical decision\u2011making, ensuring that responsibility is distributed among developers, institutions, and regulatory bodies based on their respective roles in AI implementation.

unlisted_practices: Build human intervention points into AI-driven clinical and administrative decision-making to preserve human oversight and accountability.
Train AI systems on diverse and representative datasets and audit them continuously for disparities.
Design AI systems with explainability so physicians can understand how decisions are made.
Require AI developers to disclose training data sources, model validation, and known limitations.
Subject AI systems to rigorous and continuous scientific validation.
Perform ongoing validation and real-world performance monitoring of AI used for clinical decision support.
Regulators should establish standardized evaluation frameworks for AI safety, efficacy, and clinical utility, using risk-based categorization such as IMDRF SaMD.
Educate and train physicians to critically evaluate AI recommendations and implement AI tools responsibly.
Involve physicians in leading AI implementation strategies.
Physicians and medical societies should advocate for AI systems that promote health equity.

screen.reason: This is a commentary/overview article addressing the promise, limitations, ethical concerns, physician adoption, and governance structures needed for responsible AI deployment in healthcare.
